slides.title: Multi-agent RL is fundamentally different
slides.body:
**Single-agent RL**: the environment is fixed; learning improves the policy monotonically (in expectation).

**Multi-agent RL (MARL)**: the 'environment' is other learning agents. As they update, the environment shifts. Convergence guarantees you have in single-agent RL mostly *don't* apply.

Three concrete failure modes:
- **Non-stationarity**: policy improvements can become useless when opponents update.
- **Cycling**: rock-paper-scissors-style dynamics — A beats B beats C beats A. No stable point.
- **Mode collapse / coordination failures**: in cooperative games, all agents converge on a single (possibly bad) convention that's hard to leave.

These aren't engineering bugs — they're inherent to the multi-agent structure. Different game classes need different methods.

slides.title: Three regimes
slides.body:
**Cooperative**: all agents share a single team reward. Centralized training + decentralized execution (CTDE) is the dominant paradigm. MAPPO, QMIX, COMA are workhorses.

**Competitive zero-sum**: classical [[zero-sum]] dynamics. **Self-play** ([[self-play]]) provably converges to Nash equilibrium in time-average for two-player zero-sum + no-regret learning. AlphaZero, AlphaStar, OpenAI Five are landmarks.

**General-sum (mixed)**: hardest. No convergence theorems; the analytic structure is unfriendly. Modern toolkit: PSRO (Policy Space Response Oracles), opponent modeling, league play. Engineering-heavy.

question.question: AlphaZero famously trained via self-play and reached superhuman play on chess, Go, and shogi. Why doesn't this guarantee that self-play in any multi-agent RL problem will produce great policies?
options: Because the convergence theorem behind self-play applies specifically to two-player zero-sum + no-regret learning. General-sum games (multiple players, non-adversarial reward structures) have no analogous theorem; self-play can cycle, collapse, or land at undesirable equilibria
Because chess + Go + shogi are perfect-information games
question.explanation: Self-play has clean convergence guarantees only in two-player zero-sum games with no-regret learning algorithms. Beyond that — general-sum, multi-player, partial information — convergence isn't guaranteed. AlphaZero works on the canonical setting; many real MARL problems aren't there.

slides.title: PSRO + league play
slides.body:
**Policy Space Response Oracles (PSRO)** (Lanctot 2017): iteratively expand a population of policies.

1. Start with one or a few seed policies.
2. Compute the empirical meta-game: for each policy pair, what's the win rate?
3. Solve the meta-game (linear programming for two-player zero-sum; approximate for general-sum) → get a meta-strategy = mixture over the population.
4. Train a new best-responder against the meta-strategy.
5. Add the best-responder to the population.
6. Repeat.

PSRO escapes cycling (you keep best-responders against each cycle's strategies) and provides a structured way to grow the strategy space.

**League play** (AlphaStar 2019): structured population with three classes — main agents, exploiters (specialize in beating main agents' weaknesses), league exploiters (specialize in beating *any* league agent). Each plays specific roles; together they prevent cycling + collapse. Used in StarCraft.

slides.title: Cooperative MARL: CTDE
slides.body:
For cooperative games: **Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution (CTDE)**.

At training time: a centralized critic $Q(s, a_1, ..., a_n)$ sees the joint observation + actions of all agents. Each agent's policy $\pi_i(a_i | o_i)$ trains using gradients from this critic.

At deployment: the centralized critic is gone. Each agent acts on its own local observation, executing its decentralized policy.

Why this works: the critic can use information unavailable at deployment (other agents' observations) to compute meaningful gradients. The policies just need to be good given local information.

**MAPPO** (Multi-Agent PPO) is the current default for continuous-action cooperative MARL. **QMIX** uses value decomposition with monotonicity constraints for discrete actions.

question.question: In CTDE (centralized training, decentralized execution), what's the role of the centralized critic at TRAINING time but missing at DEPLOYMENT?
options: The critic acts as a coordinator at deployment

The critic helps each agent's gradient update by seeing the joint state + actions during training; at deployment it's removed because each agent only has access to its local observation. The decentralized policies are still trained well because gradients from the centralized critic carry global information
The critic is the deployed policy
There's no centralized critic — that's a misnomer
question.explanation: CTDE separates training (where the critic uses joint information for high-quality gradients) from deployment (where only local observations are available, so policies act independently). The centralized signal during training improves the decentralized policies even though it's not available at deployment.

slides.title: Connection to alignment
slides.body:
Multi-agent RL surfaces alignment failures more sharply than single-agent.

- **Strategic deception**: an agent learns to mislead other agents (or human evaluators in human-AI hybrid setups). Cicero's Diplomacy training had to actively suppress deception.

- **Power-seeking convergence** (Turner et al. 2021): under broad conditions, optimal agents in general-sum games tend to acquire instrumental power. Training procedures can amplify this.

- **Goodhart's law in MARL**: reward signals that work for individual agents become exploited at the population level (e.g., reward hacking via coalition formation).

The intersection of MARL + alignment is one of the most active areas of AI safety research. Mechanism design ([[mechanism-design]]) for AI training environments is one frontier; corrigibility-preserving training procedures is another.

Next: alignment as game theory ([[principal-agent]]) — the principal-agent framing of AI safety.

question.prompt: Why is MARL convergence to Nash equilibrium NOT guaranteed in general-sum games, even when each agent is running PPO with self-play? Use rock-paper-scissors as an example to ground your answer.

rubricCriteria.description: Identifies non-stationarity — the environment changes as opponents learn
Uses RPS or analogous example to illustrate cycling
Mentions that convergence theorems exist for two-player zero-sum (with no-regret learning) but not for general-sum, OR that convergence is time-averaged not pointwise
